def: Ireland's armed national police force, formed as the Irish Constabulary in 1836 and given the prefix "Royal" in 1867 after the Fenian Rising; it ceased to exist in 1922 {s:wp-ric}. It was organised on military lines, "like a regiment of the army … a regimental system with an officer corps", as the narrator puts it {q:210-212} {q:T2:86}, and he says its headquarters, and Tenison Alan's office and flat, were in Dublin Castle {q:210} {q:T2:85}. Three generations of the family served in it: Tenison Alan, Bellingham Arthur and Bellingham Arthur's elder brother {q:12} {q:T2:6}. The transcripts garble the name: "the right Irish Construction" (A {q:12}), "Royal Irish Conservatory" (B {q:T2:242}), and "RUC" (B {q:T2:86}; see {t:ruc}). {s:tna-ric}

The RIC's junior commissioned rank, in charge of a police district; above it was the County Inspector {s:wp-ric}. Bellingham Arthur "never made county inspector. He was a district inspector" {q:328} {q:T2:130}. Hansard in 1887 calls the officer at Youghal both "District Inspector Somerville" and "Sub-Inspector Summerville" {s:hansard-1887} {s:hansard-1887c}. The family's "Captain Somerville" {q:316} {q:T2:125} reflects the military style of such officers.
The RIC officer commanding the force in a county, senior to the District Inspectors. {q:328} {s:wp-ric}

The official term in Irish police and government returns for crimes and disturbances, especially agrarian or political violence. Bellingham Arthur's diary refers to the riots he attended as "outrages" {q:296} {q:T2:117}; the transcript renders it "outrageous".

The British government minister who effectively ran the Irish administration from Dublin Castle, including the police. Sir William Meredyth Somerville held the post 1847–52 {q:212} {s:wp-chief-secretary} {s:wp-1st-baron}. Arthur Balfour, who answered the Commons questions about Youghal in 1887, was Chief Secretary at that time.
Shorthand for the British administration in Ireland, housed in Dublin Castle until 1922. Tenison Alan worked and lived there {q:210}.

A hereditary title (Sir …) below the peerage, passing normally to the eldest legitimate male heir. The Somerville baronetcy was created in 1748 for Sir James Somerville {q:84} {s:wp-sir-james-somerville}. {ctx}The holders were Sir James (1748), Sir Quaile, Sir James Quaile, Sir Marcus and Sir William Meredyth Somerville, the last created Baron Athlumney; his son the 2nd Baron was the 6th Baronet {s:wp-somerville-baronets}, so a successor proved today would be the 7th. A baronet's arms carry the red hand of Ulster ({t:red-hand}); succession must be proved for entry on the {t:roll-of-baronetage|Official Roll}.

A heraldic authority's formal recognition that arms a family has long used are its own, recorded in the official register, as distinct from a new grant. "In our case, our family's case, there wasn't a formal grant of arms, but there was a confirmation of arms" {q:T3:76}: the king confirming "that the arms which her father and brothers and ancestors had used were authentic and in use from time immemorial" {q:T3:78}. {ctx}The Somerville confirmation, made to Elizabeth Mary (Lily) Somerville and the descendants of Major William Somerville, is dated 2 April 1924 in the Genealogical Office's register {s:nli-arms-1924}.

Ireland's chief herald from 1552, based in Dublin Castle. "The person in charge of the arms in Ireland was the Ulster King of Arms" {q:T3:49}; Lily Somerville's confirmation was signed by "Major Sir Neville Rodwell Wilkinson … Ulster King of Arms, and Principal Herald of All Ireland" {q:T3:80}. {ctx}Wilkinson held the office from 1908 until his death in 1940; in 1943 it was joined to Norroy (Norroy and Ulster King of Arms, at the College of Arms in London), and heraldry in the Republic passed to the Chief Herald of Ireland at the Genealogical Office {s:wp-ulster-king-of-arms} {s:wp-genealogical-office}. The narrator dates the change "after 1930" {q:T3:49-50}.

term: College of Arms; kings of arms, heralds and pursuivants
def: The heralds' college in London: "it has what are called heralds" — "the chief officer, garter, king of arms. There are other kings of arms here. And then there are heralds. And then there are pursuivants" {q:T3:42-44}. The officers of arms record arms and, the narrator explains, rule on claims such as his family's to the baronetcy; his claim is in the hands of a pursuivant, "Philip Bone" {q:T3:69} {q:T3:139} {q:T3:189-191}. {ctx}The College was chartered by Richard III in 1484 (not Henry II, as the narrator says) and is at 130 Queen Victoria Street; it has thirteen officers, and James Peill is Garter King of Arms {s:wp-college-of-arms}. Phillip Bone has been Rouge Dragon Pursuivant since 2023 {s:wp-rouge-dragon}.
Entitled to bear a coat of arms. "People who have coats of arms are described as armigerous. Armiger. In other words, bearing arms" {q:T3:47-48}; "Our family have always had arms" {q:T3:48}.

term: "Crains Dieu tant que tu viveras" (family motto)
aliases: Fear God as long as you live
def: The Somerville motto, "Fear God as long as you live": "That's the family motto. Fear God as long as you live. Fear God in life", carved on the hall fireplace at Clermont {q:T3:86}. {ctx}The family's 1897 pedigree prints it in French, "Crains Dieu tant que tu viveras", with the arms: azure, three mullets or, between seven cross-crosslets fitchée argent; crest, a demi-lion rampant sable charged with a cross-crosslet and two mullets {s:visitation-1897}.

A title is dormant when the last holder dies and no heir has proved a claim, although one may exist (as opposed to extinct, when no heir can exist). The Somerville baronetcy has been dormant since January 1929 {q:174} {s:wp-athlumney}. A claimant would have to prove legitimate male descent from a baronet, which is why the legitimacy of little Archie, Archibald James's son, matters to the family's story {q:130, 168-174}. In January 1929 the press reported that "Major William A.T.B. Somerville" (Uncle Bunt) was "heir to the baronetcy" {q:T3:92-93}; no one has since been entered on the {t:roll-of-baronetage|Official Roll} ({qn:q-baronetcy-succession}).

The official register of baronets. The narrator: the baronetcy "remains dormant because … there is no member of the family on what is called the role [roll] of baronets" accepted as "the eldest son of the eldest son of the eldest son, … born in Wedlock" {q:T3:138-139}. {ctx}The Roll is maintained for the Lord Chancellor; a claimant must furnish legal evidence of succession, and a baronet not on the Roll is not entitled to the title's precedence or to be so styled in official documents {s:wp-official-roll}.

term: Settlement in tail ("heirs male of the body")
def: A settlement of land on a line of heirs in turn: "You leave your estate to the [heirs] male of your body, as long as there is an [heir] male of your body … Then it's the [heirs] female of your body, and so on" {q:T3:109}. The 2nd Baron Athlumney's estates were so settled, ending with the sons of his wife's sister, which brought Somerville to Quentin Agnew {q:T3:108-112}. A name-and-arms clause, requiring the heir to take the family's name and arms, made him Quentin Agnew-Somerville {q:T3:113} {s:wp-agnew-somerville}.
The red hand added to a baronet's arms as the badge of his rank: "That's the hand of Ulster. It's the sign of a baronet. The red hand of Ulster" {q:T3:119}, on Quentin Agnew-Somerville's shield.

term: Freedom of the City of Dublin
def: Citizenship of the city with its old privileges, which could be claimed by descent. "Bellingham also got the freedom of the city of Dublin … You could get the freedom of the city by descent … So it doesn't actually mean very much" {q:T3:17-18}. {ctx}The 1897 pedigree records the admissions of Captain William and his son Bellingham (1842), Tenison Alan (1883) and Bellingham Arthur (1893) {s:visitation-1897}.

A Bible in which a family wrote its births, baptisms, marriages and deaths. "That is the actual family Bible"; "It was said that my Captain William [Somerville] entered in all his ten children here … As they were born or baptized" {q:T3:25-27}. "So by Bible you mean just sort of a list of names, not the Holy Bible?" "No, no, this is the Holy Bible" {q:T3:27}. See {qn:q-family-bible}.

The standard reference book of the peerage and baronetage. The narrator: the penultimate edition shows the senior line; in the latest, on the advice of a professional genealogist, an American descendant of Archibald James is shown as "probably" the baronet {q:T3:116} {q:T3:130-131} {q:T3:137}. Not checked.

The narrator's name for the descendants of Archibald James Somerville's 1836 marriage to Elizabeth Crawford, who settled in America: "That is where the people I refer to as the American Somervilles" come from {q:T3:144}. He regards that marriage as bigamous and their line as illegitimate; a genealogist has advised them "that the senior American [Somerville] is the current baronet" {q:T3:131-137} ({qn:q-baronetcy-succession}).

The Norman knight with whom Bellingham Arthur's notebooks begin: "going back … to Sir Galter the Somerville [Gualter de Somerville], a nobleman knight, something, came into England" {q:T3:4-5}. {ctx}Accounts of the Scottish Somervilles make Sir Gualter "a Norman knight and companion of William the Conqueror", rewarded with Whichnour (Wychnor) in Staffordshire and Aston Somerville near Evesham {s:wp-lord-somerville}. {int}Bellingham Arthur gave two of his children the Staffordshire names Whichnour and Alrewas, and named a son Gualter {p:pat|(Uncle Pat)}.

Peerage created in 1863 for Sir William Meredyth Somerville, 5th Bt (with the UK barony of Meredyth in 1866). Both became extinct, and the baronetcy dormant, when the 2nd Baron died childless on 8 January 1929 {q:174} {s:wp-athlumney}.

variants: the Louth, that's the County Louth Militia
def: County-based part-time regiments, reorganised in Ireland by the Militia Act of 1793 into 38 county and city regiments, with Protestant officers; the units saw heavy service in 1798 {s:wp-irish-militia}. The narrator compares them to the later Territorials {q:56-58} {q:T2:29}. Captain William served in one after leaving the regular army: transcript B is explicit, "he was in the Louth, that's the County Louth Militia" {q:T2:29}, where A garbles it as "the Laos … country … militia" {q:56}. A compiled genealogy agrees {s:winters-p67}. It was also the regiment of his father-in-law Henry Bellingham {s:lf-bellingham}. Family tradition puts his earlier service in the South or North Cork regiment {q:54-56} {q:T2:27-28}.
Britain's volunteer reserve force (from 1908). The narrator uses it to explain what the earlier militia was: "local troops" {q:58}.

The most junior infantry officer rank. Until purchase was abolished on 1 November 1871, most British army commissions were bought: "a young man going into the army generally purchased or was given an ensign ship, which is a junior officer, a cadet ship" {q:34} {q:T2:17}. {s:wp-purchase}

The two army colleges: the Royal Military College, Sandhurst, trained infantry and cavalry officers {s:wp-sandhurst}; the Royal Military Academy, Woolwich, trained officers of the Royal Artillery and Royal Engineers {s:wp-woolwich}. Bunt, Jim and Pat "all followed normal army careers, going to Sandhurst or Woolwich, the two army colleges, when they were in their late teens" (transcript B {q:T2:137}; A: "sand test or college" {q:346}).

Nickname for the Royal Regiment of Artillery. Jim was "a gunner, Royal Artillery" {q:366}; Reginald may have transferred to the Gunners in Italy {q:362}; "Gunners Venture" in Kenya was reportedly founded by gunner officers {q:498}. The transcript renders "gunner" as "Ghana".
A soldier or officer of the Royal Engineers. Aunt Eddie's husband "was a sapper, that is, the Royal Engineers" {q:256}.

Line infantry regiment (formerly the 6th Foot) in which both Pat and Reginald served in the First World War {q:358, 360, 394}. Its 1st Battalion was in the retreat from Mons in 1914 {s:wp-royal-warwick}.

Infantry regiment named by the narrator as Bunt's in the First World War {q:364}. A published source instead lists him as Royal Artillery when he commanded a Machine Gun Corps battalion in 1919 {s:mgc-8bn}; see {qn:q-bunt-regiment}.
Corps formed in 1915 to operate machine guns; its 8th (Special) Battalion, under Lt-Col W.A.T.B. Somerville, was sent to North Russia in 1919 {s:mgc-8bn}.
Distinguished Service Order, a decoration for officers, usually for leadership under fire. A published source gives Bunt the DSO {s:mgc-8bn}; the narrator does not mention it.

A gallantry award for officers of the rank of captain or below and for warrant officers, instituted on 28 December 1914 {s:wp-mc}. Pat (Gualter) "got the MC" after his escape {q:450} {q:T2:173}; the IWM record (seen in search results) dates it to 1919 {s:iwm-gualter}.

Allied military intervention at Murmansk and Archangel in 1918–19, first to protect stores and the Eastern Front, then in support of anti-Bolshevik forces during the Russian Civil War {q:364} {s:wp-north-russia}.
The two-week fighting withdrawal of the British Expeditionary Force after the Battle of Mons (23 August 1914), in which many British soldiers were captured {q:442} {s:wp-great-retreat}.
The Third Battle of Ypres (July–November 1917), notorious for mud and casualties {q:356} {s:wp-passchendaele}.
The war of 1807–14 in Spain and Portugal against Napoleon, in which Wellington's army stormed Badajoz in April 1812 {q:44} {s:wp-badajoz}.

The influenza pandemic of 1918–20; in Ireland its three waves came in June–July 1918, October–November 1918 and February–spring 1919 {s:dcc-flu}. Bellingham Arthur died "of the flu that was then going around" in 1916 (20 January 1916, according to a compiled genealogy {s:winters-p68}); the narrator "always thought" it was the Spanish flu but doubted it, rightly {q:10-12} {q:T2:4-5}.

variants: The far in the four courts
def: The destruction of the Public Record Office of Ireland on 30 June 1922, at the start of the Civil War, with the loss of most pre-1922 Irish public records including 19th-century censuses and many wills and church registers {q:4} {q:T2:2} {s:irishtimes-pro}. Genealogists value anything copied before 1922, such as Bellingham Arthur's notes. The Beyond 2022 project is reconstructing what it can {s:tcd-beyond2022}.

Members of the Irish Republican Brotherhood (founded in Dublin on 17 March 1858) and its American wing, the Fenian Brotherhood, seeking Irish independence by armed revolution {s:wp-fenian}. The narrator says they were "at large" in the 1880s and 1890s, when Bellingham Arthur attended riots {q:296} {q:T2:117}.

A tenant strategy of 1886–91: if a landlord refused a reduced rent, tenants withheld the rent and paid it into a National League fund used to support evicted tenants. Smith-Barry bought up the Ponsonby estate at Youghal to defeat it {s:wp-plan-of-campaign}. The Youghal riot of March 1887 arose from the arrest of a priest believed to be a trustee of such a fund {s:ballymacoda-1887}.

A formal notice by the prosecution that it will not proceed with a charge. On 8 September 1887 the Attorney General for Ireland confirmed to the Commons that a nolle prosequi had been entered at the Cork Assizes in "the Queen v. Sub-Inspector Somerville and Constable Ward" {s:hansard-1887-sep8}; in May he had said he saw "no grounds to advise a prosecution" {s:hansard-1887c}. A local history describes the men as "eventually acquitted" {s:ballymacoda-1887}. The narrator says, more exactly, that Captain Somerville was "reinstated, but … never formally acquitted" {q:T2:126-127} {q:322}.
A coroner's inquiry into a sudden death. A coroner's jury could name those it held responsible; at Youghal in 1887 it returned "wilful murder" against the officer and constable {s:ballymacoda-1887}.

Irish estates were mostly let to tenant farmers; disputes over rent and eviction ("the agrarian problems in this country") drove much of 19th-century Irish politics {q:86-88} {q:T2:42}. The transcript has "talented" for "tenanted".

A pre-marriage deed securing property or income for a wife and children. Captain William "put one half of his interest in the lands into his marriage settlement", from which Eliza drew an income {q:88-90} {q:T2:43}.
A woman paid to breast-feed another's baby. Captain William paid "a succession of wet nurses" for little Archie {q:162}.
Pregnant. Archibald James "had got a girl into the family way" {q:16}.
Help in getting established; the narrator explains it as money or help "to settle down in Canada" {q:30-32}.
Quoted from Captain William's diary: little Archie was "frequently, quote, brought out, close quote" to Cumry, i.e. brought to visit {q:162}.
A feckless, idle person. Said of William Henry Somerville {q:104}.

Marrying into a family whose money came from commerce or manufacture rather than land or the professions, once thought socially beneath gentry. Hence Mr Clinch burnt his name off the beer barrels {q:240-244}.

The evangelical wing of Anglicanism (here the Church of Ireland), wary of ritual and strongly anti-Catholic. Bellingham Arthur "was also very low church … He would have had a fit if he knew that any of his descendants married a Roman Catholic"; "he never sent any of his children to school because schools were smutty places" (transcript B {q:T2:134-136}; A {q:338-344}). The interviewer compares it to the Reformed churches of the Continent {q:342} {q:T2:135}.
A country house with gardens and a modest acreage, not a working estate; how the narrator characterises Clermont's 70 acres {q:582}.

Many Irish country houses were burned in 1920–23, and many more sold, stripped and demolished in later decades. The narrator places Ardrass among them {q:94-96}, and the interviewer recalls the burnings {q:600-602}.
A person's permanent legal home, which decides which country taxes and administers their estate. The Irish and English Revenue disputed Margaret Somerville's {q:548}.
The person appointed by a will to administer an estate. Bunt was executor of his mother's estate {q:560}.

The Visitation of Ireland, edited by Joseph Jackson Howard and Frederick Arthur Crisp (1897–1918): privately printed pedigrees, supplied by the families themselves, that often reproduce family signatures. In the first recording the narrator shows "an entry in a journal called Crisp's" with the facsimile signatures of Captain William and Eliza {q:124} {q:T2:54-55}. In the second he explains it: "The families themselves sent in the information, so they're not authoritative in many ways. It is what the family believed to be the case. This is what my grandfather sent in" {q:T3:13-14}, and the family's copy carries handwritten additions by his grandfather and father {q:T3:23-24}. {ctx}The Somerville pedigree is in volume 1 (1897), pp. 64–65, "Somerville of Clermont, co. Wicklow" {s:visitation-1897}, with Reginald's birth in the additions to volume 2 {s:visitation-additions}. It names all ten of Captain William's children, which settles the eighth son ({qn:q-eighth-son}).

Commercial genealogy website. The interviewer's online tree is "based off of other people's research" and records {q:120}; the Johnson ancestry in this archive comes from it and is unverified {q:520-524}.

Ireland's heraldic authority and genealogical archive. It was based in Dublin Castle until 1981, moved in 1987 to part of the former Kildare Street Club premises, and became formally part of the National Library of Ireland in 1997 {s:wp-genealogical-office}. The narrator remembers the moves in the reverse order {q:272-276} {q:T2:108-109}.

Dublin's principal gentlemen's club for the Protestant landed class; its former building at the bottom of Kildare Street later housed the Genealogical Office {q:274}. In the second recording the narrator mentions a talk by the Garter King of Arms "in the Kildare Street Club" the following evening {q:T3:65-66}.

A separate Somerville family of Castletownshend, West Cork, "very naval" and "further off related" {q:472} {q:T2:183}. They include the novelist Edith Somerville and still live at Drishane, whose present owner the narrator names as "Thomas, Tom Somerville" {q:T2:184} {s:drishane-southernstar}.
The family name, of Scottish origin. Transcription software garbles it badly; search for any of the variants listed here.

The family of Castle Bellingham, Co. Louth, of English (Westmorland) origin, from which Eliza Bellingham came {q:20, 28}. After her marriage it became a recurring Somerville first name: her son Bellingham, her grandson Bellingham Arthur, and great-grandsons William Arthur Tenison Bellingham, James Aubrey Henry Bellingham and Hugh Roger Bellingham {q:26}.

Anglo-Irish family name. Eliza Bellingham's mother was Elizabeth Tenison and her brother was Henry Tenison Bellingham {s:lf-bellingham}; the name passed to her son Tenison Alan Somerville and great-grandson W. A. Tenison B. Somerville. The transcript spells it "Tennyson", like the poet.
Wicklow gentry family of Clonmannon, spelled out by the narrator: T-R-U-E-L-L {q:248}.

The surname of Elizabeth, believed to be the mother of little Archie: "Breaky" in transcript A {q:110}, "Brakey" in B {q:T2:50}. The narrator did not spell it. Breakey is an established surname in Monaghan and Cavan, pronounced much like "Brakey".
Family name for William Arthur Tenison Bellingham Somerville {q:218}. Its origin is not explained.

Names for Edeline ("Adeline") Somerville: "known as Eddie or Teddy. Because as children, they couldn't say Eddie. They said Teddy. So she continued to be called Tettie by most of the family, but I've never called her anything other than Eddie" (transcript B {q:T2:90-91}; A: "Tete" {q:226}).

Names for Gualter Hugh Roger Bellingham Somerville. "Pat or Paddy, or [Gualter], I always called him. We as a family have always called him Paddy, but he was known as Pat because he was the Irishman in the regiment" (transcript B {q:T2:142}). Transcript A's "Penny" and "quarter" {q:360} are mishearings of Paddy and Gualter.
A Nazi regional party leader. Said in jest of a family member, the household's organiser of gadgets: "James is known as the gauleiter" {q:586} {q:T2:234}.
A momentary lapse of memory; the narrator's self-deprecating phrase {q:32, 42}.
The narrator's offer to show the interviewer the family portraits {q:46}.
Ireland's indigenous nomadic ethnic minority, historically called "tinkers" (now considered offensive). The term appears in local hearsay the narrator repeats about Rathnew {q:584}.

"There was a company called Gunner's Venture. That was a company started by Gunner officers after the First World War who wanted a job" {q:T2:193} {q:498}. Reginald, "not a gunner", got a job with it managing coffee plantations near Nanyuki {q:T2:194-195} {q:500}. No independent record of the company has been found under that name ({qn:q-gunners-venture}).

In the 1920s Kenyans objected to the reservation of the Kenya "White Highlands" for European settlers, especially British war veterans {s:wp-kenya-colony}. Reginald went out in 1920 with an artillery officers' company to manage coffee near Nanyuki {q:T2:193-195} {q:498}.
The Religious of Christian Education, who acquired Clermont and ran a school there from 1956 {q:532} {s:irishaesthete-clermont}.

The granite book-rooms in Lutyens's Irish National War Memorial Gardens, Islandbridge, which hold the illuminated volumes of Ireland's Memorial Records 1914–1918 (artwork by Harry Clarke); the memorial is dedicated to 49,400 Irish soldiers {s:wp-war-memorial-gardens}. The narrator recalls "pillars" in which "all medals and things are all stored" {q:T2:207-208} {q:526-528}.

The burning of much of Cork city centre by British forces, including Auxiliaries of the RIC, on the night of 11–12 December 1920, during the War of Independence {s:wp-burning-cork}. Raised by the interviewer {q:602-606} {q:T2:242-243}.

Northern Ireland's police force from 1922 to 2001, founded as the successor to the RIC {s:wp-ruc}. Transcript B has the narrator say "It was like the RUC. It was like a regiment of the army", which may be a genuine comparison, and then "Tennyson Allen was an officer of the RUC" {q:T2:86}, which must be a mishearing of RIC, since the RUC did not exist until 1922. Transcript A has neither {q:210-212}.
